## Design

### 2026-10-27: # starting with the schematic!

**1.5h**

# starting with the schematic!

I've come up with the main idea for what I want my Starmatch to be, and it'll just be a simple matching game that'll test your reaction time. There'll be four groups of 6 neopixels in each section of a PCB, and each group will have its own switch. There'll be an OLED in the center that displays what colour to press, and you just have to press the colour in a certain amount of time (probably around 2 seconds). Then, you just keep going! I'll maybe add a special effect or sound if I have time, but I don't want to complicate it too much since I don't have that much experience in coding or LEDs.

For now, I've just come up with the schematic, which I mostly just used the guide for.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/95758776baae53e104f0d9c540386ed3c180bf84bc86d88e7624446b76319da9.png)

I'm using the XIAO-ESP32-C3 and I simply connected a long chain of 24 neopixels together. I also added the capacitor on each one, so essentially the module looks like this:

![Screenshot 2026-10-26 234112](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/b6aec9b220096aed48879dada93cff360ae8de4cf81e211c967fda9cd5209402.png)

I then added a level shifter, which will shift the power from 3.3 V to 5V.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/d52b9e9a631464c589673722685886b779e1399e89937af6091d8f8d3ecd6828.png)

Finally, I added the switches and the 4 pin connector for the OLED.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/5c5657bc7725cff0e4d53f4843600569337d9f3f94beb2d8f474c4b7c4eadec5.png)

tl;dr is that I made the full schematic, including the neopixels, level shifter, switches, and OLED.

### 2026-10-28: # adding footprints :( and the "start" of the layout

**1.3h**

# adding footprints :( and the "start" of the layout

Before I started anything today, I added in the 4 SK6812-MINIs because it's nice to have some under-key lighting for each of my switches. To do this, I just added in each one and attached them to the same long strip that I have, since I read that it's actually easier to code with enumerated Neopixels connected to one pin compared to several different pins. So this is what my schematic was looking like:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/524603dec36be472828fa3fc274f9de4395efc64d3fcedd556d6454b62adea7a.png)

After that, I started working on the footprints for everything, which took FOREVER to do. The first issue was that KiCad automatically assigned the LED footprints onto the capacitors, which was completely wrong. I didn't know that, however, so I was super confused when I entered into the PCB editor and saw double the amount of LEDs I put in. I was also confused when I saw that the capacitors had their own footprint in the footprint table provided in the guide, but because KiCad auto-assigned the capacitors to the LED footprint, I thought I just didn't have capacitors for some reason. I spent a long time trying to fix that, before I eventually realized...

Another issue was that the footprint table in the guide doesn't have all the footprints, and I'm assuming some were self-explanatory, but not for me. Of course, I recognize that this is a great way to teach beginners to make their own projects, however, saying this is "easy" is an overstatement... Anyways, I had to figure out what footprint to put for the switches, XIAO, and 4 pin connector. For the 4 pin connector, I just did the same thing as last week and made it vertical, since I read that it would be easier to solder. For the switches, I just used the Kailh Choco switch footprints that were used in the MIDI tutorial last week, since I know they already have a hole cut out for the SK6812-MINIs. For the XIAO, KiCad auto-assigned a footprint, but I couldn't figure out why it was yellow:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/928e75d66beeb2c42ef15b63952a5f9644e4218a9001c1a8aec2c6fd87ec2b73.png)

Yellow usually indicates that the footprint hasn't been fulfilled yet, but I thought it was fulfilled since it showed a footprint attached to it. Additionally, when I put it into PCB editor, I didn't even have a microcontroller! I also remember seeing a comment on #half-life concerned about not having the footprint for the XIAO, so I thought I just didn't even have the footprint in my library. So, I went onto the XIAO github and downloaded the zip for all its footprints, and added that in. I think it fixed the problem, but I genuinely have no way of knowing if the guide doesn't provide me any visual indicator of knowing if the footprint's correct or not.

Additionally, it doesn't provide a footprint for the 22uF capacitor, so I had to search up what footprint it should be. Here's what I did though:

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/a3ea843009f6ba94549d9b9e973efeb0f0b1f739fbb8bfb0651991f974750c1e.png)

After all these issues with the footprints, I thought I had everything prepared for my layout, but when I started arranging everything, I realized it may be easier to have 4 LEDs in a cluster compared to the 6 I originally intended to have. I wanted to have the LEDs in a star shape, but I'm using 5 mm x 5 mm LEDs which are bigger (for easier soldering) and makes the star shape less practical. So I'm switching to using just 4 LEDs per cluster, meaning that I'll only need 16 LEDs for the whole thing. For the next step, I'll just be laying out everything and changing the schematic to have 16 LEDs compared to 24.

tl;dr is that I added 4 under-key LEDs for my switches, and I had a huge problem with the footprints because I couldn't figure out what the guide wanted (the footprint table wasn't too helpful), and I'm updating my schematic and layout to have 4 LEDs per cluster instead of my original 6

### 2026-10-28: # the layout!

**1.7h**

# the layout!

As I said in the previous entry, I'm updating it to have 4 LEDs per cluster instead of 6. So I updated the schematic and the footprints, as well as updating all the reference names (this isn't necessary but I changed them anyways because it looks a lot nicer).

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/4292f5052961bd881f28ded801bd7dfb71083675ec77cf93e17d7ed2c522ce12.png)

I also set up the layout in the PCB editor!

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/19edea4b0b1f4df755f635f7d9bac932b9bb895590fe89a503f90cbd937f6b26.png)

I already had an idea of what layout I wanted to make, with the OLED and the microcontroller in the center, with 4 switches and 4 clusters of LEDs on each side (top, left, bottom, right). This was relatively easy to implement, since all I needed to make sure of was that I had to every capacitor right next to its LED. I also made sure to add the level shifter  and the bulk capacitor right next to their respective pins.

The challenging part of this was making sure that my PCB was under 100mm x 100mm. My MIDI isn't, and it's probably going to be pretty expensive, so I want to make sure that this one IS under the limit. This took a lot of squishing in and trying my best to make every part fit together, especially because I wanted to add an edge cut and it was already on the brink of being over the limit. I eventually managed to do so, though (it's around 96mm x 96mm)!

I also originally wanted the shape of my PCB to be a star, like the name Starmatch suggests. However, I realized that wouldn't be possible if I wanted my PCB to be under 100mm x 100mm. So, I had to switch it to being this clover shape, which I do think is more unique! I also didn't really know how to make curves in the edge cuts (I know you can use the Arc tool or the Bezier Curve tool, but I find them difficult to use), so I chose a simple vector on Canva, converted it from PNG to DXF, and imported it. However, the name doesn't really make sense anymore, so I'll probably switch it to something like Clovermatch or Luckymatch.

It looks super cool in 3D too!!

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/448938748fc7bc02d8f6a58994ea30b3aaa10b26fca3c42a7bbd7d0a52525183.png)

tl;dr is that I set up the schematic for 16 LEDs and made the layout in the PCB editor, making sure that my PCB is under 100mm x 100mm

### 2026-10-28: # routing...

**1h**

# routing...

I started with routing after finishing the layout of my PCB, and I thought I would at least be a little better with making it neat because I've routed before with my MIDI, but turns out, not so much... The first thing I did was add in the GND pour on the back, which I've already done countless times so it was pretty simple. Since KiCad automatically clips the GND pour to your edge cut even if the filled in shape doesn't match the edge cut, I didn't have to worry about the curved lines. I was a little confused on why the guide specifically said to put the GND pour on the back, since most of my LEDs are on the front (I have 16 on the front and 4 on the back). However, I was eventually able to realize that you can just use vias to get the GND from the back, and having a GND pour on the back is a lot cleaner and reduces the risk of isolated islands (since there's less components on there).

I tried to route everything cleanly and nicely by putting vias as close to possible to all my GND connections, but it ended up not looking great.

![Screenshot 2026-10-28 132616](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/900ebc96eb8676fb4e2e8a78a9ecb1a8bf7c4a061bc85018a890aeddef3024dc.png)

This is mostly because the guide requests the 5V and GND lines to be 0.8mm, which makes them extra chunky and hard to maneuver around. I tried again but the result wasn't much better :(

![Screenshot 2026-10-28 133210](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/5aa2c24de089903ee9ed5630335b099c2445697125c247ac6ae249dc55e52582.png)

I also eventually realized that I had ordered everything the wrong way. It's much easier to put SW1 on the right side rather than on the top, since the bulk capacitor is on the left side, which essentially means all my work was for nothing!!

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/f2c4c38c267f20be370a5349cff6a1736f12442d7764d532766bdacc515350ed.png)

I'll just rearrange and route everything next.

tl;dr is that I started routing everything but it was hard to get it clean, and then I realized I arranged everything incorrectly

### 2026-10-29: # adding in the graphics and text!

**0.8h**

# adding in the graphics and text!

This is always a step that takes me so much more time than necessary because I'm super indecisive and can't choose what graphics or text I want to put on my PCB, but I think I've more or less streamlined my process because I've had so many problems with it for my past 2 PCBs.

For example, when making my Starbie, the main problem I had was that the image was unclear since KiCad can only choose between black or white, so low contrast images don't really look like anything. So, I made sure to look for high contrast images where it is pretty much only one colour, such as outlines. For this project, I made all of my graphics cross-stitch patterns! When making my MIDI, the other problem was the scale of the image. You can't scale footprints easily in the editor, so I believed that you could only change the size through a website online, which was such a hassle and took way too much time to download, enter it in, and redownload. However, I only just noticed that KiCad has a built in scaler when converting images... though, to give me the benefit of the doubt, I normally download all the images in the image converter instead before testing them as footprints...

So, it took me less time than usual to make all my footprints! I decided to just go with a bunch of random patterns I saw on Pinterest. To keep up with my theme of having Wingdings text on my PCBs, this one says: "Luck is predictable; the harder you work, the luckier you get." - Brian Tracy 2001

### 2026-10-30: # some more firmware

**1.4h**

# some more firmware

I worked on some more of the firmware by adding in the OLED code and refining some of the code I did yesterday! Most of it came from sources online, and these three are especially helpful:
* https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nHECoycpmEY
* https://docs.circuitpython.org/en/latest/shared-bindings/time/
* https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-lrJ0fy0xm0

For starters, I imported some more libraries, and I pretty much just got the same ones as I did for the MIDI and the random module (for randomly selecting colours). The set up for the OLED was basically the same as well!

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/86538ec3ba13bee4cfdfb7e0e936d3c327e58cbfbae52e1417acb2b1c1ae4ee3.png)

I also made the main game loop by using a while loop, and then also adding a while loop inside the main game loop for each iteration. To start the main game loop, all you have to do is just press one of the four buttons (since it uses PULL_UP, this is determined by not button_value). When the main game loop starts, the key backlights turn on and it selects a random colour. Then, it starts the iteration, which is basically each round of choosing a colour and giving you your reaction time.

After talking with one of my friends who is more experienced with Python, I also found that my code from yesterday wouldn't work because you can't have an else and elif next to each other, as the else ends the previous if and the elif can't stand on its own. So instead of each key getting its own module like before, I just made one else for all the keys.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/3194a5f786e6aeccbce2d2a3035b97280a1e526c7b42bd94c19ee0a7fe43af5f.png)

I also added a simple time elapsed calculator that starts the time after it chooses a colour and ends it when you press a key. After you press a key, your selected_colour will be the new colour you chose. Once it detects that your selected_colour is no longer empty, then the iteration will end. If you chose the correct colour, it'll display the time elapsed (i.e., your reaction time), and displays some custom messages based on how fast you were!

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/59e9ec8233d62d639271fda60559e4af644ed800ac58e89825be5f84ad7b666f.png)

I'll maybe change the milliseconds later, since those times are based off a classic reaction time game where you just have to press  a key. Since my game also tests your hand-eye coordination and cognitive ability (as you also have to press the right colour), the times might be different and I'll do some tests once I get the actual board.

I also might be adding a new function if I can to change the LED colours so they aren't just one colour each time (so button 1 isn't always red all the time), and it'll add some more functionality.

tl;dr is that I worked on more of the firmware by adding in all the OLED code and the game code, but I also had to edit a lot of my previous code

### 2026-10-31: # finishing up the firmware!

**1h**

# finishing up the firmware!

As I said in my previous entry, I want to make it so that the NeoPixels switch each round so that the player can't just memorize where each key is and what colour they correspond to, since that defeats the whole purpose of having a display. It also means that the display won't just stay static for each round and it'll actually change and have an impact on the game itself!

To do that, I had to create a list of the button colours and just randomly shuffle it. Instead of making each key correspond to red, it will correspond to its specific index in the shuffled list. For example, if red is index 2, then the third key (with index 2) will switch to red. I initially held off on this idea because I thought it wouldn't be possible (for some reason I thought that each button is locked to what data it transmits), but I eventually figured it out. So all I had to do was, for each index, transmit the correct colour:

![Screenshot 2026-10-31 135006](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/0458d1266737c3271355e4acd020d448d1c8e4b6dc076996b5c48e80892f37df.png)

So the button_colour is the list of colours, and it'll onboard the index (i) of that list. I also made it the same for switching to the light colours when the button is pressed, but my code looked SUPER UGLY! It just looks like it repeats unnecessarily and just looks really bad, but I guess it'll still function correctly. The problem is that the NeoPixels only read RGB values and I have each button colour stored as a string ("red", "green", "blue", "yellow") so it won't work if i just onboard the button colour. Instead, Google recommended me to create a dictionary where each string corresponds to an RGB value and I can just onboard the string with the dictionary.

![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/af8f4061721d49d86f20f744111be7d83c14f44ab4627bbdff884fbeeef3b0bc.png)
![image](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/Fkyd7BnPhA7YS61rynMPOy9Dgjdve6I4/f01b29aae723b4b750b52d409f660a732fe13e47652ce105b47449eae90e8de7.png)

Other than that my code stayed the same, so now I've finished the firmware!

tl;dr is that I finished my firmware by adding two dictionaries and making so that each LED lights up to different colours each time by corresponding its string to an RGB value
